learn.b: In Java all code sits inside a class. The class name usually matches the file name, so class Hello goes in Hello.java. Curly braces { } mark where a class or method starts and ends.

When you run a Java program, the JVM looks for a method called main and starts there. Its first line must be exactly public static void main(String[] args). Without it the program has no starting point.
Java is compiled first. The command javac Hello.java turns your source file into bytecode in Hello.class. Then the command java Hello runs that bytecode on the Java Virtual Machine.
Java is case sensitive, so main and Main are different names. Every statement ends with a semicolon. Lines inside braces are indented to make the code easy to read.

int holds whole numbers. double holds decimals. boolean holds true or false. char holds one character in single quotes. long holds very big whole numbers and needs an L at the end, like 5000000000L.
After a variable exists you can change it with =, without writing the type again. When you copy a primitive into another variable, you copy the value, so the two stay independent.
Put final before a variable to make it a constant that cannot change. Names start with a letter, have no spaces, and by convention use camelCase like playerScore.

learn.b: A while loop repeats its block as long as the condition is true. The condition is checked before every round, so the body may never run. Make sure something inside changes the condition, or the loop never ends.
A for loop packs three parts into one line: a start, a condition and an update. It is perfect when you know how many times to repeat.
A do-while loop runs the body first and checks the condition afterwards. That means it always runs at least once, which is handy for menus and input checks.
break leaves the loop immediately. continue skips the rest of the current round and jumps to the next one. Loops can also be placed inside each other, called nested loops.

Valid indexes go from 0 to length - 1. Using any other index stops the program with an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Arrays can also have two dimensions, like int[][] grid = new int[3][3].

learn.b: A method is a named block of code you can run many times. In a simple program write static before it. You give it a return type, a name and parameters in parentheses.
A method that returns nothing has the return type void. A method with another return type must use return to send a value back, and return also ends the method immediately.

Parameters are the variables in the method header. Arguments are the actual values you pass when calling it. Java passes a copy of primitive values, so changing the parameter does not change the caller's variable.
Several methods can share a name if their parameter lists are different. Java picks the right one by looking at the arguments you pass. This is called overloading.
learn.code:

static double add(double a, double b) { return a + b; }

learn.b: A constructor is a special method that runs when you use new. It has the same name as the class and no return type. It is the place to give fields their first values.

A getter returns a private field and a setter changes it. A setter can check the new value first, for example refuse negative ages. Outside code uses these methods instead of the field.

learn.b: A class can inherit fields and methods from a parent class using extends. The child gets everything the parent has and can add more. A Java class can have only one parent.

A child can replace a parent's method by writing a method with the same name and putting @Override above it. The keyword super refers to the parent, so super.speak() calls the parent's version and super(...) calls its constructor.
A variable of the parent type can hold a child object. When you call a method, Java runs the version of the real object. One call can behave differently for different children.

learn.b: An ArrayList is a resizable list. Import java.util.ArrayList and put the item type in angle brackets. Use add to append, get(i) to read, size() for the length and remove(i) to delete by index.
A HashMap stores key and value pairs. put adds or replaces a pair, get finds the value for a key, containsKey checks a key and size counts the pairs. Putting an existing key again replaces its value.
An exception is an error that happens while the program runs. Put risky code in try and handle the problem in catch. When an error happens, Java jumps from the risky line straight to catch.

A finally block runs whether or not an error happened, which is good for cleanup. You can raise your own error with throw new IllegalArgumentException("message"). Common exceptions are NullPointerException and ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
